screenings.description: Mitchell’s Detroit-shot sophomore film, winner of the Next Wave award at Austin’s Fantastic Fest in 2014 and the breakout horror phenomenon of the following year, is a work of potent sexual dread, in which erotic congress transmits something much worse than a dose of clap: the attentions of a spectral, shape-shifting entity that pursues the afflicted with methodical single-mindedness, a pursuit that ends in terrible carnage. Enigmatic and unsettling, its thick atmosphere of paranoia incalculably added to by a soundtrack courtesy electronic musician Disasterpiece (Rich Vreeland), per Pitchfork “a score that announces when something is about to happen, only to suddenly upend expectations and leave the room on edge.”

screenings.title: Kaili Blues
screenings.description: Chinese filmmaker Bi Gan’s award-winning directorial debut is an audacious work that announced a major new filmmaking talent. Country doctor Chen Sheng sets out on a train journey to search for his brother’s abandoned child, only to find himself in a dreamlike world where the boundaries between past, present, and future—and between fantasy and reality—are porous. This remarkable visual achievement, which feels as singular and alien as the films of Apichatpong Weerasethakul, was shot in the mining village Kaili, the director’s birthplace, and incorporates poetry he’s been writing since he was a teenager.

screenings.title: Lady Killer
screenings.description: Grémillon was still in the employ of Berlin’s UFA Studios when he began shooting this adaptation of an André Boucler novel which stars Jean Gabin as a Don Juan of the French Foreign Legion who sets his sights on seducing Mireille Balin—and accidentally falls in love for real. The atmospheric work of cinematographer Günther Rittau (The Blue Angel) connects Grémillon’s film to the legacy of German expressionism, while the electric reunion of Pépé le Moko co-stars Gabin and Balin and the film’s pervasive air of tragic romantic fatalism show an affinity with French poetic realism. Distributor: Grasshopper Film

screenings.title: The Band Wagon
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1953, 111 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Fred Astaire, Cyd Charisse, Oscar Levant, Nanette Fabray, Jack Buchanan. One of the crowning glories of American musical cinema, Minnelli’s The Band Wagon is a triumph of the form, recycling the old backstage theater formula into a winsomely graceful celebration of the virtues of popular art. Playing a version of himself as an aging Hollywood star, Astaire leads a cast that includes Fabray and Levant, standing in for the film’s real-life writers Betty Comden and Adolph Green; Buchanan, incarnating a pretentious, blowhard actor-director à la Orson Welles; and Charisse, playing the ballet dancer turned show business ingénue she then was. The Band Wagon elevates these Hollywood traditions to new heights of technical display (“A Shine on Your Shoes”), self-reflexive comedy (“That’s Entertainment!”), and sublime visual poetry (“Dancing in the Dark”). screenings.title: Peggy
screenings.description: Dir. Charles Giblyn, Thomas H. Ince. 1916, 70 mins. U.S. Restored DCP courtesy of the Academy Film Archive. With Billie Burke, William Desmond, William H. Thompson, Charles Ray. Though most of the films featuring silent cinema star Billie Burke (the future Glinda the Good Witch in The Wizard of Oz) have been lost, Peggy was restored by the Academy Film Archive in 2018. Starring Burke as an independent-minded, wealthy young woman from New York who causes a stir when she moves to a remote village in Scotland, Peggy captures Burke’s dynamism, joie de vivre, and comedic brilliance. Burke was also well known as a fashion plate, and this film showcases the actress in her trend-setting one-piece “Billie Burke” pajamas, as well as an array of beautiful clothing provided by some of the most renowned couture designers of the period, including Lucile, Lady Duff Gordon. This screening is presented in conjunction with Bard Graduate Center Gallery’s exhibition Goddesses in the Machine: Fashion in American Silent Film (on view now until January 3, 2027), which features a short excerpt from the film. This screening offers the rare opportunity to see the film in its entirety, and it will be introduced by Goddesses in the Machine co-curators Michelle Finamore and Emma Cormack. screenings.title: The Saga of Anatahan
screenings.description: Visionary Josef von Sternberg had once been a feared and revered presence on the Paramount Studios lot, but after one too many clashes over his obsessive perfectionism rendered him all but unemployable, and a falling out with Howard Hughes over his Jet Pilot, “Jo” went independent, directing, writing, shooting, and narrating this sublimely artificial picture, shot entirely on a Kyoto soundstage, about a dozen Japanese seamen stranded on a Pacific Island with one woman—unaware that World War II has long since ended, and that a little war of their own is in the making. A favorite film of one of von Sternberg’s students during his tenure teaching at UCLA, none other than Mr. Mojo Rising himself, Jim Morrison.

screenings.title: Blue + Chinese Series
screenings.description: Over the same, unceasing monochromatic sea of blue, Yves Klein’s patented “International Klein Blue,” the voices of Jarman and collaborating actors (including Tilda Swinton and Nigel Terry) read a poetic text by the director in which he muses on the physical and mental deterioration wrought by the ravages of AIDS, as well as the endless implications of the color blue. Jarman would be gone within a year, but he left behind one of the great final films, a vibrant work of courage and clarity in the face of oblivion. Screens with Brakhage’s Chinese Series, a long-contemplated short work inspired by Chinese ideograms completed in the filmmaker’s dying days.

screenings.title: 67 Bombs to Enid + Q&A
screenings.description: Between 1946 and 1958, the U.S. detonated 67 nuclear bombs in the Marshall Islands, contaminating the region and leaving generations of Marshallese facing illness. Decades later, many of the survivors and their descendants are building a new life in the United States.

screenings.title: The Inugami Family
screenings.description: Based on Seishi Yokomizo’s 1951 bestseller The Inugami Curse, adapted before and after Ichikawa’s 1976 blockbuster, but arguably never bettered—mystery/melodrama The Inagami Family takes place in the fallout following the death of the wealthy patriarch of the eponymous clan, whose members start to drop off like flies in the most unnatural of ways, leaving detective Kosuke Kindaichi (Kōji Ishizaka, who would play the same role for Ichikawa in four more Kindaichi films) on a race to ferret out a culprit before the reading of the will. Simmering resentments, a veritable army of closeted skeletons, and more twists than a super-coaster make this a must-see for the whodunnit addict.

screenings.title: Time Indefinite
screenings.description: His complicated relationship with his aging surgeon father, his settling into married life and fatherhood in early middle-age—these subjects, the sort of foundational building blocks of life so central as to often be taken for granted, are at the center of McElwee’s autobiographical documentary Time Indefinite, a film that brings a dry, laconic humor to its very serious meditations on mortality, family, and spirituality. “A rich and compelling cinematic experience… Conveys a sensuous appreciation of the physical world that is so acute that the environment is almost as important as the people… Communicates a sense of the elusive moment in all its complexity and richness being captured.” —The New York Times

screenings.title: Top Stripper
screenings.description: Directed with remarkable levity, and vibrant, on-location cinematography, Morita’s Top Stripper is an irreverent take on the seishun eiga, raising questions of spectatorship as a young boy falls in love with a dancer. Treating sex as a mere fact of life, Morita captures his subjects' personal lives with heartfelt candor.

screenings.description: Thirty-four days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss.

screenings.title: Paradox on 72nd Street
screenings.description: Over the course of three years, Gene Searchinger filmed pedestrians, joggers, buskers, bench sitters, stoop sleepers, and countless other types of New Yorker (whom the narration describes as “exaggerated Americans”) at the corner of Broadway and 72nd St. Visually, the film presents an hour-long stream of individuals, each with their own unfathomable inner mindscape, who together comprise “the collective”; the paradox referred to in the title is narrator Lewis Thomas’s assertion that, “It is in our genes to live together and to depend on each other, to be our individual separate selves and at the same time the working parts of others.” Thomas, a biologist and the film’s co-writer, shares narrating duties with the anthropologist Philip Slater, both of whom offer meandering philosophical notes on individualism in American society.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: ACE Presents: Day Night Day Night
screenings.description: Before her epic My Undesirable Friends made Loktev one of the most-discussed figures in contemporary nonfiction, there was Day Night Day Night, the director’s riveting fiction feature debut, closely following 48 hours in the life of an unnamed young woman, played by an entrancing Luisa Williams, as she makes preparations to detonate herself in a Times Square suicide bombing in service to an unknown cause. Shot with remarkable immediacy and adroitness by cinematographer Benoît Debie, best known for his collaborations with Gaspar Noé, and lent a sense of subtly rising tension that reaches a point of near-suffocation by editor Michael Taylor, Loktev’s austere film—and its brooding, taciturn leading lady—exert a sinister undertow pull of fascination.

screenings.title: Woman on the Night Train
screenings.description: New English Subtitles by Japan Society. A baroque fantasy by way of Vadim and Buñuel’s Diary of a Chambermaid, Noboru Tanaka’s Woman on the Night Train is a gothic work replete with decadent, atmospheric imagery and unravelling psyches.

screenings.title: Remake
screenings.description: Setting out to document the process of turning his 1985 nonfiction classic Sherman’s March into a fiction film—while reeling from the death of his 27-year-old son, Adrian—McElwee, in his first film following a 14-year hiatus, gives an enormously tender cinematic eulogy that is also something of a summation of his filmmaking life, describing among many things the tenuous tightrope walk between necessary consideration of practical, commercial concerns and a relentless striving towards honesty and integrity. All of the elements that constitute McElwee’s peculiar genius—the diarist’s warts-and-all self-revelation, the paring away of inessentials in pursuit of universal truths, the off-kilter comic vision—are to be found in spades in the many layers that comprise the extraordinary Remake.

screenings.title: The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces
screenings.description: This film emerged from city planner William H. Whyte’s years of research into pedestrian behavior and city dynamics, conducted as part of his Street Life Project. His research resulted both in a film and a book, both of which closely analyzed the functioning of public spaces in various cities, above all in NYC. The book quickly became a classic text within the realm of city planning, and remains beloved not only for the wisdom and elegance of its insights, but for its disarmingly unpretentious, no-nonsense, and often flat-out funny tone. The film version fully embodies all the qualities of the book, and adds one special feature: Whyte’s own voice. Sounding very much like Jimmy Stewart’s city planner cousin, Whyte delivers the narration with an often-self-deprecatory folksiness that’s charmingly at odds with the stentorian tone of most educational films. The film is also effectively a work of street photography. Whyte and his team’s dedication to observing – and recording – the actual behavior of city dwellers, and their sharp eye for the behaviors and gestures that are most revealing of city life, result in a film that is – almost incidentally – a classic city symphony. THE SOCIAL LIFE OF SMALL URBAN SPACES is one of the great films about that strangest of creatures – the city dweller – in its natural habitat.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Talk To Her
screenings.description: A travel writer’s burgeoning relationship with a famed female matador is violently interrupted when she falls into a coma after a bullring tragedy, and while waiting at her hospital bedside, he meets a male nurse keeping a similar vigil over a comatose ballet dancer. Only Almodóvar could come up with such a deliciously ridiculous premise for a film, and only Almodóvar could make it into a melodrama of unusual emotional power.

screenings.title: Tokyo Sonata
screenings.description: Kurosawa’s reputation was made as perhaps the most formidable figure in the “J-horror” boom, so his about-face into contemporary-set shomin-geki melodrama à la Yasujirō Ozu was an unexpected—but not unwelcome—surprise… though beneath the placid surface of Tokyo Sonata, sinister stirrings are very much visible. Salaryman Teruyuki Kagawa, newly out of work, struggles to keep up the illusion of employment for his family, consisting of one son who lights out to join the US Army, another with a not-so-dirty secret of his own (the scamp is taking piano lessons), and a wife (Kyōko Koizumi) who finds an unlikely solution to her unhappy domestic existence when she’s kidnapped by a home invader. Winner of the Prix Un Certain Regard at the 61st Cannes Film Festival.

screenings.title: Taxi Driver
screenings.description: “Suck on this!” A pure distillation of needling isolation, inadequacy, and anguish, all roiling in the tortured gut of Robert De Niro’s insomniac cabbie Travis Bickle, who cruises all night through a stygian, steam-choked Manhattan, nursing his fears and hatreds. A defining picture of New York City in 1976, and a movie that is wrenched straight from the unquiet psyche of its screenwriter, exorcizing his personal demons.

screenings.title: What Is the City but the People?
screenings.description: “In 1969 the Department of City Planning attempted to shore up support for its various [development] projects with a multipronged, multimedia public relations blitz. At its center was the publication of a six-volume book, ‘The Plan for New York City’ (1969), which articulated the commissioner’s vision for the metropolis to stem the flight of the middle classes to the suburbs and revitalize urban space. The plan was presented in synopsis form as a propagandistic documentary produced by the Department and co-directed by John Peer Nugent and Gordon Hyatt. Featuring some flashy cinematography from New York location shooter-extraordinaire Arthur J. Ornitz [THE CONNECTION; MINNIE & MOSKOWITZ; SERPICO], WHAT IS THE CITY is an idiosyncratic document of the city in the late 1960s, offering a wide panorama of places and spaces, narrated by one of the plan’s ghost writers, William H. Whyte [THE SOCIAL LIFE OF SMALL URBAN SPACES]. The film flits between footage of and discussion about ‘urban crisis’ (uprisings, poor housing stock, street violence) and purported city-led remedies. Viewed today, the film is both a curious relic of failed urban policy and an index of just how wedded city authorities were (and remain) to the idea that the manipulation of public perception is key to urban governance.” –FILM AT LINCOLN CENTERCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Rocky Horror Picture Show (live)
screenings.description: An outrageous assemblage of the most stereotyped science fiction movies, Marvel comics, Frankie Avalon / Annette Funicello outings and rock 'n' roll of every vintage. The madcap musical mayhem begins when rain-soaked Brad and Janet take refuge in the castle of a mad scientist from outer space who is about to unveil his greatest creation - and have a bit of fun with his reluctant guests! Join Tim Curry, Barry Bostwick, Susan Sarandon and rock star Meatloaf in the most popular cult classic of all time.​

screenings.title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
screenings.description: Pasolini’s final film remains one of the most shocking ever made. Set during a waning fascist Italy’s dark days amidst World War II, Salò updates the writings of Marquis de Sade to create a repugnant tale of four wealthy libertines who kidnap a group of teenage boys and girls and enact horrific humiliations and violence upon them. A formally and conceptually brilliant, if relentlessly nauseating, portrayal of man’s most debased instincts and the capitalist systems that allow them to thrive. Per Pasolini, “The most sincere thing I could do at that moment was to make a film about a mode of sexuality whose joyousness is a compensation for repression—a phenomenon that was about to come to an end, forever.”

screenings.title: It Follows
screenings.description: Mitchell’s Detroit-shot sophomore film, winner of the Next Wave award at Austin’s Fantastic Fest in 2014 and the breakout horror phenomenon of the following year, is a work of potent sexual dread, in which erotic congress transmits something much worse than a dose of clap: the attentions of a spectral, shape-shifting entity that pursues the afflicted with methodical single-mindedness, a pursuit that ends in terrible carnage. Enigmatic and unsettling, its thick atmosphere of paranoia incalculably added to by a soundtrack courtesy electronic musician Disasterpiece (Rich Vreeland), per Pitchfork “a score that announces when something is about to happen, only to suddenly upend expectations and leave the room on edge.”

screenings.title: Poetry
screenings.description: Mija (Yun Jung-hee) has been tasked with raising her troubled teenaged grandson, Jong-wook, while her daughter, Jong-wook’s single mother, works in far-off Busan. When her capacity as a caregiver is threatened by a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s, Mija begins to study poetry composition at the local cultural center—first inspired by beauty in the natural world, then, when Jong-wook is mired in shameful scandal, inspired by new depths of disappointment and pain. Written specifically for Yun, a leading light of ’60s and ’70s South Korean cinema who gives an achingly vulnerable performance, Lee’s poignant, penetrating drama was awarded Best Screenplay at Cannes in 2010.

screenings.title: The Royal Ballet: the Nutcracker (2026)
screenings.description: At a cosy Christmas party, young Clara meets the mysterious magician Drosselmeyer, who gives her a nutcracker doll. When the guests have departed and the house is asleep, Clara sneaks downstairs in search of the doll. Instead, she finds Drosselmeyer, who whisks her away on a journey into a whole world of enchantment: fantastical landscapes of flurried snow and glittering confection where toys come alive and the magic never stops. Peter Wright’s production of this festive family favourite sparkles to the wondrous swell of Tchaikovsky’s orchestral score, alongside the glow and grandeur of Julia Trevelyan Oman’s period designs.

screenings.title: Wild Boys of the Road
screenings.description: “By the time Eddie breaks down and cries, ‘I’m sick of being hungry and cold! I’m sick of freight trains!’ both the romantic notion of the train and the idle fantasies of boyhood have been demolished. Suffering is everywhere and there’s no one to blame for it. Though this was a Pre-Code film, its intended ending was still too bleak for producer Jack Warner. If the new ending feels off, it’s a credit to the mounting sense of desperation Wellman built with the rest of the film, where there are no easy answers.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue

screenings.description: “Trains often spell escape for characters in Ray’s films; Pather Panchali’s image of children running through a field to chase a locomotive is one of his most poignant. Nayak reverses the situation somewhat. For fading movie star Arindam Mukherjee (played uncomfortably close to type by matinee idol Uttam Kumar), the train he boards to avoid a flurry of bad press ends up returning him, nightmarishly, to himself.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue

screenings.description: “This landmark film by pioneering director Julie Dash forever changed my thinking about the Great Migration, not to mention Gullah culture. Her key participation in Anthology—foregrounding the contributions of the remarkable Ann Lowe and Eartha Kitt—reveals Dash’s distinctive voice and ongoing commitment to centering the lives of Black women.”—Sylvia Yount, Lawrence A. screenings.title: Cinexpérimentaux: a Meeting with Abigail Child
screenings.image: https://anthologyfilmarchives.org/uploads/Encounter_Child with The Future Is Behind You copy.jpg
screenings.description: Part of Michel Amarger and Frédérique Devaux’s ongoing series of documentary portraits of those who further the cause of experimental cinema in the 21st century (other subjects have included the filmmakers Nicolas Rey, Rose Lowder, and Stephen Dwoskin, as well as scholars, distributors, and curators such as Vivian Ostrovsky, Pip Chodorov, the Light Cone cooperative, and others), A MEETING WITH ABIGAIL CHILD represents a deep dive into the life and work of Child. Encompassing several in-depth interviews, copious footage from her films past and present, and revealing glimpses of the artist at work, the documentary is an essential supplement to Child’s own filmography.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Leviathan
screenings.description: Setting out on the high seas of the North Atlantic aboard a Massachusetts-based commercial fishing trawler, Castaing-Taylor and Paravel produced one of the most mesmerizing, visually distinctive, and startlingly immediate documentaries of the 21st century, using the unique agility of their lightweight GoPro cameras to capture perspectives unlike anything theretofore seen in cinema, from gull-like views of the vessel to plunges into the slimy viscera of the day’s catch. “The density of aural and visual stimuli overwhelms—and liberates.”—Melissa Anderson, The Village Voice

screenings.title: Still Life + Train-Trains #2: A Bypass
screenings.description: A program of two formally adventurous trainspotting films from the Middle East. Stephan’s memory piece Train-Trains #2: Bypass follows the weed-choked rails of a former train line, an extension of the Orient Express that once linked Lebanon to Palestine, which lives on in the memories of those who reside near its long-abandoned stations; Saless’s Still Life, a key film of the early Iranian New Wave and winner of the Silver Bear at the 24th Berlin International Film Festival, observes the daily lives of a longtime crossing guard (Zadour Bonyadi) at a remote train station and his wife, whose well-worn routine will be upended by an unexpected development.

screenings.title: Third Avenue: Only the Strong Survive
screenings.description: “This Emmy Award-winning documentary tells the stories of six ‘ordinary’ people who live or work along New York City’s Third Avenue, which runs for sixteen miles through Manhattan, Brooklyn, and the Bronx, cutting through the complex social strata of the city to reveal wildly different economic and ethnic subcultures. The subjects speak for themselves, offering candid glimpses into the disparate worlds of a junkyard dealer who steals cars, a Bowery denizen and the wife he abandoned, a welfare mother living in a condemned building with her five children, a sex worker, a devout Puerto Rican factory worker, and an aging Italian barber and his wife. This unsentimental portrait of the uncommon lives of common people is a subjective sociological study of survival in urban America.” –DCTVCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Woods are Wet
screenings.description: An adaptation of Marquis de Sade’s Justine, Tatsumi Kumashiro’s gothic work of depravity follows a young woman who stumbles upon a rural countryside inn governed by sadistic perversions.

screenings.title: The Celebration
screenings.description: The opening salvo in Dogme 95’s all-out assault on cinematic artifice, revolutionary in its emancipated use of the Sony DCR-PC7 Handycam, Vinterberg’s scorched earth melodrama/farce takes place during a gathering of the extended Hansen clan at a family-run hotel to mark the 60th birthday of solid burgher patriarch Helge (Henning Moritzen)—an event that takes a turn for the chaotic when Helge’s eldest son, Christian (Ulrich Thomsen), accuses his father of molesting both himself and his recently deceased twin sister during a dinner table toast. Abrasive, volatile, savagely funny, and endlessly inventive, one can scarcely feel indifferent towards such a blood-on-the-walls affair as this.

screenings.title: Lady Killer
screenings.description: Grémillon was still in the employ of Berlin’s UFA Studios when he began shooting this adaptation of an André Boucler novel which stars Jean Gabin as a Don Juan of the French Foreign Legion who sets his sights on seducing Mireille Balin—and accidentally falls in love for real. The atmospheric work of cinematographer Günther Rittau (The Blue Angel) connects Grémillon’s film to the legacy of German expressionism, while the electric reunion of Pépé le Moko co-stars Gabin and Balin and the film’s pervasive air of tragic romantic fatalism show an affinity with French poetic realism. Distributor: Grasshopper Film

screenings.title: Last Cabaret
screenings.description: Focused on a family-run cabaret soon to be shuttered, Shusuke Kaneko’s (Summer Vacation 1999) elegiac Last Cabaret would be the penultimate film in Nikkatsu’s erotic line—a bittersweet requiem for the end of Roman Porno.

screenings.title: Every Contact Leaves a Trace
screenings.description: “For most of her life, filmmaker Lynne Sachs has saved every business card ever placed into her hand – more than 600 fragments of chance encounters, fleeting conversations, and unexpected connections. Drawing on the forensic principle that every contact leaves a trace, Sachs selects seven cards and follows them back into the lives they represent. A German woman reckons with history, an artist reflects on government surveillance, a forensic scientist searches the cards for DNA, and when memory reaches its limits, cinema fills in the gaps. Blending documentary, speculation, performance, and personal reflection with remarkable grace, Sachs transforms an ordinary archive into a meditation on memory, history, and the invisible ways we shape one another’s lives.” –Bryan Wendorf, CHICAGO UNDERGROUND FILM FESTIVAL“Sachs reveals her strength: she captures beauty in the mundane, elevates the casual to poetry, and shows that even the most fleeting encounter leaves a lasting legacy.” –Martijn Smit, CINEMAGAZINE“Sachs extends the interpersonal scale of her inquiry into a more expansive awareness. Her on-screen interlocutors serve as mirrors into her own wandering mind, a gesture toward entanglement reminiscent of Chris Marker’s reflexive SANS SOLEIL. With Sachs, we learn that to be in relation is to come to terms with one’s capacity to do harm and to accept that we might leave imprints that elude our awareness entirely.” –Delaney Holton, SCREEN SLATE“A deeply personal meditation on memory, history, and chance encounters that exemplifies Sachs’s uniquely lyrical approach to nonfiction filmmaking.” –SCREEN MAGAZINELynne Sachs will be here in person for all screenings! screenings.title: Stalker
screenings.description: Tarkovsky’s stunning, haunted sepia-toned sci-fi masterpiece follows a scientist and a writer who, living in a broken-down totalitarian dystopia, recruit the help of a “Stalker”—a kind of post-apocalyptic Sherpa—to guide them on a voyage of self-discovery, passing through the bleak, otherworldly Zone in hopes of finding therein a haven that will fulfill their secret desires. An enigmatic, austere, and utterly immersive experience that combines religious allegory and political prophesy, and has kept cinephiles debating its meaning for some 50 years.

screenings.title: The Inugami Family
screenings.description: Based on Seishi Yokomizo’s 1951 bestseller The Inugami Curse, adapted before and after Ichikawa’s 1976 blockbuster, but arguably never bettered—mystery/melodrama The Inagami Family takes place in the fallout following the death of the wealthy patriarch of the eponymous clan, whose members start to drop off like flies in the most unnatural of ways, leaving detective Kosuke Kindaichi (Kōji Ishizaka, who would play the same role for Ichikawa in four more Kindaichi films) on a race to ferret out a culprit before the reading of the will. Simmering resentments, a veritable army of closeted skeletons, and more twists than a super-coaster make this a must-see for the whodunnit addict.

screenings.title: Brave New York
screenings.description: “BRAVE NEW YORK is a free-form documentary that loosely chronicles the last 12 years [as of 2004] of intense change in the East Village ‘hood.’ From the reopening of a newly curfewed Tompkins Square Park and Wigstock in ’92, to the destruction of the cherished Loisaida Community Gardens, to the yuppie invasions of the dot com years, to the present era, indelibly stamped with post 9/11 grief, this durable, lusty neighborhood survives in spite of a real estate gold rush that has excluded all but the well-to-do. The movie’s main voices are those of the artists and street people whose wisdom and commentaries upon the dominant culture give us pause amidst the speedy approach of a ‘Brave New World.’” –Richard SandlerCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Urban Video Project
screenings.description: “Urban Video Project (UVP) [was] a media education program [that ran] at Satellite Academy (Forsyth St.) from the mid-1980s through the 90s, providing students with the opportunity to craft half-hour documentaries as a cultural preservation effort, exploring the culture of Black and Latino people in their communities and the legacy of the African diaspora. screenings.title: Every Contact Leaves a Trace
screenings.description: “For most of her life, filmmaker Lynne Sachs has saved every business card ever placed into her hand – more than 600 fragments of chance encounters, fleeting conversations, and unexpected connections. Drawing on the forensic principle that every contact leaves a trace, Sachs selects seven cards and follows them back into the lives they represent. A German woman reckons with history, an artist reflects on government surveillance, a forensic scientist searches the cards for DNA, and when memory reaches its limits, cinema fills in the gaps. Blending documentary, speculation, performance, and personal reflection with remarkable grace, Sachs transforms an ordinary archive into a meditation on memory, history, and the invisible ways we shape one another’s lives.” –Bryan Wendorf, CHICAGO UNDERGROUND FILM FESTIVAL“Sachs reveals her strength: she captures beauty in the mundane, elevates the casual to poetry, and shows that even the most fleeting encounter leaves a lasting legacy.” –Martijn Smit, CINEMAGAZINE“Sachs extends the interpersonal scale of her inquiry into a more expansive awareness. Her on-screen interlocutors serve as mirrors into her own wandering mind, a gesture toward entanglement reminiscent of Chris Marker’s reflexive SANS SOLEIL. With Sachs, we learn that to be in relation is to come to terms with one’s capacity to do harm and to accept that we might leave imprints that elude our awareness entirely.” –Delaney Holton, SCREEN SLATE“A deeply personal meditation on memory, history, and chance encounters that exemplifies Sachs’s uniquely lyrical approach to nonfiction filmmaking.” –SCREEN MAGAZINELynne Sachs will be here in person for all screenings! screenings.title: Bill Moyers Journal: Rosedale: the Way It Is
screenings.description: Amid the recession of the early 1970s, Black families began moving into nearly all-white Rosedale, a working-class Queens neighborhood just across the border from wealthy Nassau County. This film documents the explosive racist violence that followed: Tony and Glenda Spencer, a Black mother and father whose house was bombed twice but who refused to leave, anchor the film. “We’re going to stay here,” Glenda says. “Definitely going to stay.” (They did; as of 2019, she still lived in her home.) Moyers also follows a “home referral service” calling itself R.O.A.R. (Return Our American Rights) that aimed to keep Black people from becoming property owners in Rosedale, while moonlighting as a white supremacist terrorist gang. ROSEDALE was given a second life in 2019 when Sola Olosunde, a Hunter College graduate student in urban planning, sent out a viral tweet featuring the film’s most grotesque sequence, in which several Black children are assaulted by a group of white children. “Black and white alike in the Rosedales of America have been abandoned, condemned together to economic apartheid by a system that rewards the people who can afford to get out, and condemns to bitter, consuming rivalry those left behind,” Moyers opines. “It’s a travesty.”Introduced by photographer and public historian Sola Olosunde.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn, the construction site manager, and Cal, a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone, Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. screenings.title: Third Avenue: Only the Strong Survive
screenings.description: “This Emmy Award-winning documentary tells the stories of six ‘ordinary’ people who live or work along New York City’s Third Avenue, which runs for sixteen miles through Manhattan, Brooklyn, and the Bronx, cutting through the complex social strata of the city to reveal wildly different economic and ethnic subcultures. The subjects speak for themselves, offering candid glimpses into the disparate worlds of a junkyard dealer who steals cars, a Bowery denizen and the wife he abandoned, a welfare mother living in a condemned building with her five children, a sex worker, a devout Puerto Rican factory worker, and an aging Italian barber and his wife. This unsentimental portrait of the uncommon lives of common people is a subjective sociological study of survival in urban America.” –DCTVCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

SIMPLY JOHANNE deftly explores her complex and audacious life through archival footage, interviews with loved ones, and performances of her writings by three contemporary actresses. screenings.title: New Yorkers + Before the First Word
screenings.description: This program pairs two films, made a decade apart, that vividly demonstrate the vibrant, distinctive, and sometimes paradoxical nature of New York City’s neighborhoods: at once strikingly diverse and worldly, and yet close knit and self-enclosed. NEW YORKERS (1971), by filmmaker Michael Blackwood (who during his long career made several films about the city, as well as dozens of documentaries about artists, architects, and musicians), sets its sights on the Upper East Side, and in particular on the area in and around East 77th Street. BEFORE THE FIRST WORD (1982) – a co-production between WNET and the educational organization Learning Designs, and ostensibly a film designed as a teaching tool for journalism students – is set seventy-something blocks to the south, in Greenwich Village. Both films capture the degree to which their respective neighborhoods have developed specific cultures, institutions, and local networks to create a kind of shelter from the vertiginous, unceasing forces of change that animate Manhattan – and the degree to which they’re nevertheless unmistakably subject to the evolution that is the fate of all city neighborhoods, and to the more aggressive, inorganic tides of gentrification that have increasingly transformed the city over the past fifty years.Michael BlackwoodNEW YORKERS1971, 29 min, 16mm-to-DCPTom SimonBEFORE THE FIRST WORD1982, 29 min, videoTotal running time: ca. 60 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Bouchra
screenings.description: With a lived-in granularity and unmistakable visual style, BOUCHRA, the feature debut from acclaimed visual artists Meriem Bennani and Orian Barki (best known together from their 2020 web series 2 LIZARDS), is a singular portrait effortlessly towing the line between documentary, visual art and resonant family drama. Deeply felt, surprisingly sexy and formally adventurous, Bennani and Barki’s distinctive debut forges new ground that “will make it a classic of queer cinema for years to come” (Next Best Picture).

screenings.title: The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces
screenings.description: This film emerged from city planner William H. Whyte’s years of research into pedestrian behavior and city dynamics, conducted as part of his Street Life Project. His research resulted both in a film and a book, both of which closely analyzed the functioning of public spaces in various cities, above all in NYC. The book quickly became a classic text within the realm of city planning, and remains beloved not only for the wisdom and elegance of its insights, but for its disarmingly unpretentious, no-nonsense, and often flat-out funny tone. The film version fully embodies all the qualities of the book, and adds one special feature: Whyte’s own voice. Sounding very much like Jimmy Stewart’s city planner cousin, Whyte delivers the narration with an often-self-deprecatory folksiness that’s charmingly at odds with the stentorian tone of most educational films. The film is also effectively a work of street photography. Whyte and his team’s dedication to observing – and recording – the actual behavior of city dwellers, and their sharp eye for the behaviors and gestures that are most revealing of city life, result in a film that is – almost incidentally – a classic city symphony. THE SOCIAL LIFE OF SMALL URBAN SPACES is one of the great films about that strangest of creatures – the city dweller – in its natural habitat.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: What Is the City but the People?
screenings.description: “In 1969 the Department of City Planning attempted to shore up support for its various [development] projects with a multipronged, multimedia public relations blitz. At its center was the publication of a six-volume book, ‘The Plan for New York City’ (1969), which articulated the commissioner’s vision for the metropolis to stem the flight of the middle classes to the suburbs and revitalize urban space. The plan was presented in synopsis form as a propagandistic documentary produced by the Department and co-directed by John Peer Nugent and Gordon Hyatt. Featuring some flashy cinematography from New York location shooter-extraordinaire Arthur J. Ornitz [THE CONNECTION; MINNIE & MOSKOWITZ; SERPICO], WHAT IS THE CITY is an idiosyncratic document of the city in the late 1960s, offering a wide panorama of places and spaces, narrated by one of the plan’s ghost writers, William H. Whyte [THE SOCIAL LIFE OF SMALL URBAN SPACES]. The film flits between footage of and discussion about ‘urban crisis’ (uprisings, poor housing stock, street violence) and purported city-led remedies. Viewed today, the film is both a curious relic of failed urban policy and an index of just how wedded city authorities were (and remain) to the idea that the manipulation of public perception is key to urban governance.” –FILM AT LINCOLN CENTERCLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

WIZARDS is pure, unrestrained Bakshi, filled with freaky characters, psychedelic backgrounds, and hallucinatory rotoscoping.Preceded by:Tommy Turner THE MAGICIAN 1998, 9 min, 16mmWIZARDS is paired with Tommy Turner’s THE MAGICIAN, a transgressive take on the rituals of ceremonial magic.Total running time: ca. 95 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Paradox on 72nd Street

screenings.title: Brighton Beach
screenings.description: At once a charming portrait of the diverse residents of a unique New York City neighborhood, a vibrant time capsule of the city at the very beginning of the 1980s, and a penetrating exploration of the social and political dynamics of a rapidly changing community, BRIGHTON BEACH is a long-lost gem of documentary cinema that has been newly restored by IndieCollect. Directed with great empathy and perceptiveness by Carol Stein & Susan Wittenberg, BRIGHTON BEACH captures the Brooklyn neighborhood known as the poor man’s paradise – a city by the sea down the street from the Coney Island boardwalk. Interspersing interviews with the neighborhood’s residents – including the Soviet Jews who had begun arriving in large numbers at the time – with archival footage of the area fifty years earlier, the film is both a portrait of a very particular time and place as well as a study of the ways in which urban communities function, cohere, and continuously transform themselves.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Film About A Father Who + Q&A
screenings.description: With a nod to the Cubist renderings of a face, Sachs’ cinematic exploration of her father offers simultaneous, sometimes contradictory, views of one seemingly unknowable man who is publicly the uninhibited center of the frame yet privately ensconced in secrets. With this meditation on fatherhood and masculinity, Sachs allows herself and her audience to see beneath the surface of the skin, beyond the projected reality. As the startling facts mount, she discovers more about her father than she had ever hoped to reveal.

screenings.title: The Magician
screenings.description: Long though lost until its mysterious recovery in the late 20th century, Rex Ingram’s THE MAGICIAN remains one of Hollywood’s most extravagant explorations of the occult. It features Paul Wegener as the hypnotist Oliver Haddo (a character modeled on Aleister Crowley), who seeks out the blood of a virgin for his alchemical experiments in creating life. The film is based on W. Somerset Maugham’s 1908 novel of the same name, which Crowley vituperatively accused of plagiarism.Preceded by:Kenneth Anger INVOCATION OF MY DEMON BROTHER 1969, 12 min, 16mmTHE MAGICIAN will be shown alongside Kenneth Anger’s dense and mesmerizing INVOCATION OF MY DEMON BROTHER, which features the Moog drones of Mick Jagger and the Satanic presence of Anton LaVey. Anger held Ingram and his films in great esteem. He claimed that his grandmother, a wardrobe mistress, had worked on a number of his productions; through her stories of the time, the young Anger “became fascinated by this other period when nobody talked on the screen and when there were these magical, mythical images.”Total running time: ca. 100 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: The Tempest
screenings.description: Jarman’s rendition of Shakespeare’s final work becomes an emblematic pageant of Renaissance magic, influenced by the director’s study of the real-life Elizabethan sorcerer Dr. John Dee, with poet Heathcote Williams as the brooding Prospero. “I hope to capture something of [the] mystery and atmosphere of the original without descending to theatrics,” Jarman wrote in his notes, adding that “There are films where magic works.”Preceded by:Percy Stow THE TEMPEST 1908, 12 min, 35mm-to-DCPThis film – one of the earliest visualizations of Shakespeare’s play – was directed in 1908 by British trick-film pioneer Percy Stow.Total running time: ca. 110 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

Preserved by Anthology Film Archives with support from the National Film Preservation Foundation.A cautionary tale about past-their-prime thespians caught up in a typically Kucharian vortex of madness.Len LyeTUSALAVA (1929, 10 min, 16mm, silent)TRADE TATTOO (1937, 5 min, 35mm)RHYTHM (1957, 1 min, 16mm)FREE RADICALS (1958/79, 4 min, 16mm)A giant of experimental animation, Len Lye was born in New Zealand in 1901. He moved to England in the 1920s and subsequently to New York in 1944, where he spent the last 40 years of his life. A pioneer of “scratch” or “direct” filmmaking, Lye used various tools to mark patterns, shapes, and images directly onto the film’s surface, and often explored the dynamic energy of abstract images propelled into life by lively jazz scores or Pacific-inspired rhythms.Total running time: ca. 55 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Wizards
screenings.description: Ralph Bakshi’s anti-fascist passion project, developed over decades and released prior to his LORD OF THE RINGS, mixes sci-fi and fantasy to tell the story of a far-future Earth where magic and fairies have returned in the wake of nuclear holocaust. These forces of good must battle an evil wizard who attempts to control the world by reviving the forbidden technologies of war. WIZARDS is pure, unrestrained Bakshi, filled with freaky characters, psychedelic backgrounds, and hallucinatory rotoscoping.Preceded by:Tommy Turner THE MAGICIAN 1998, 9 min, 16mmWIZARDS is paired with Tommy Turner’s THE MAGICIAN, a transgressive take on the rituals of ceremonial magic.Total running time: ca. 95 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: Ghassan Salhab(POSTHUMOUS) / (POSTHUME)2007, 31 min, DCP. In Arabic with English subtitles.“Not long after the Israeli attack of 2006, Ghassan Salhab directed this filmic essay; its images are both absent and present witnesses to an unexpected war. A cinematographic musing on contemporary Lebanon and a wager on the impossibility of recounting the violence of a bruised country, whose ghosts reappear from the ruins and stare at the screen, before disappearing in cross-fade.” –VISIONS DU RÉELGhassan SalhabNO TITLE2025, 42 min, DCP. In Arabic with English subtitles.“[NO TITLE is] a car-bound survey of utterly devastated sites in South Lebanon following the 2024 Israeli airstrikes. In many respects this film can be viewed as an extension of [Salhab’s CONTRETEMPS (2024)], an afterword necessitated by ongoing escalations beyond the cinema screen. It is not to reveal too much about NO TITLE to cite its closing statement, a gnomic endnote that hints at the unfathomably endless horrors of Israel’s war: ‘still today’.” –ALCHEMY FILM & ARTSTotal running time: ca. 75 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.description: Disney’s underrated adaptation of the first title in T.H. White’s classic series The Once and Future King relates the coming-of-age of a young King Arthur, here named Wart, and his training by the wizard Merlin. screenings.title: Leonora in the Morning Light + Q&A
screenings.description: In the early 1930s, painter Leonora Carrington, a rebel against social expectations, joins the surrealist movement and its iconic figures like André Breton and Salvador Dalí in Paris. A whirlwind love affair with artist Max Ernst confronts her with her inner demons. During the war, Leonora flees to Mexico and finally empowers herself. Today Leonora Carrington is one of the highest selling female painters worldwide, next to Frida Kahlo and Georgia O’Keeffe.

screenings.title: Narrow Rooms: Terence Davies Trilogy
screenings.description: Terence Davies did not have a happy childhood, and his early adulthood was plagued by guilt and anguish over his homosexuality. But film became his outlet for self-expression, and in this trilogy of black-and-white short films, Davies brilliantly laid out the anguish of his bleak early years. In CHILDREN, Davies faces homophobic bullies at school and an abusive father at home. In MADONNA AND CHILD, the adult Davies spends his days visiting his aging mother, and his nights pursuing guilt-inducing sadomasochistic sex. DEATH AND TRANSFIGURATION allows Davies to imagine the circumstances of his twilight years and recall slightly fonder moments from his childhood. Though these brilliant films were underappreciated on their release, they announced Davies as a major talent who became one of the greatest gay filmmakers of all time. What better time could there be than the Christmas season to catch this unrelenting exploration of gay Catholic guilt and existential dread?“The trilogy did the rounds of the international festival circuits and was often seen – in the States in particular – as an unnecessarily pessimistic piece, receiving limited arthouse distribution as a result. In a ‘glad to be gay’ climate, the insecurity, guilt and downright loneliness so astutely expressed in these films was an unfashionable stance. Because Terence dared to show the pain of growing up Catholic and homosexual in working-class Liverpool in the ’50s and early ’60s, the films were not celebrated enough. Terence once told me that when he recognized his homosexuality he knelt in prayer for so long that his knees bled – this pain is conveyed in the spirit of his films.” –Jennifer Howarth, SIGHT AND SOUND, 1994CHILDREN (1976, 43 min, 16mm-to-DCP)MADONNA AND CHILD (1980, 30 min, 16mm-to-DCP)DEATH AND TRANSFIGURATION (1983, 23 min, 16mm-to-DCP)Total running time: ca. 100 min.CLICK HERE TO BUY TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Ec: George Landow, Aka Owen Land
screenings.description: “The unique contribution of Land’s work lies in the fusion of intellectual reason and, significantly, the humor that distances it from the supposedly ‘boring’ world of avant-garde film. Having explored the basic properties of the celluloid strip itself in early works such as FILM IN WHICH THERE APPEAR…, his attention turned to the spectator in a series of ‘literal’ films that question the illusionary nature of cinema through the use of word play and visual ambiguity. His work often parodies experimental film itself by mimicking his contemporaries and mocking the solemn approach of film theorists and scholars.” –Mark Webber, TWO FILMS BY OWEN LANDFLEMING FALOON (1963, 6 min, 16mm)FILM IN WHICH THERE APPEAR EDGE LETTERING, SPROCKET HOLES, DIRT PARTICLES, ETC. (1965-66, 5 min, 16mm, silent)DIPLOTERATOLOGY (1967/78, 7 min, 16mm, silent)THE FILM THAT RISES TO THE SURFACE OF CLARIFIED BUTTER (1968, 9 min, 16mm)INSTITUTIONAL QUALITY (1969, 5 min, 16mm)REMEDIAL READING COMPREHENSION (1970, 5 min, 16mm)WHAT’S WRONG WITH THIS PICTURE? screenings.description: “The few facts that are known about Maclaine are, at best, sketchy. He was a published poet, a sort of down and out San Francisco bohemian who later became one of the psychic casualties of that scene. His last years were spent at Sunnyacres, a state mental hospital in Fairfield, California. These films, along with Ron Rice’s, are clearly the most significant work to come out of the beat period.” –J.J. screenings.title: Ec: Walden (diaries, Notes, and Sketches)
screenings.description: “Since 1950 I have been keeping a film diary. I have been walking around with my Bolex and reacting to the immediate reality: situations, friends, New York, seasons of the year. On some days I shot ten frames, on others ten seconds, still on others ten minutes. Or I shot nothing. When one writes diaries, it’s a retrospective process: you sit down, you look back at your day, and you write it all down. To keep a film (camera) diary, is to react (with your camera) immediately, now, this instant: either you get it now, or you don’t get it at all.” –Jonas MekasCLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!

screenings.title: Ec: Reminiscences of a Journey to Lithuania
screenings.description: Preserved by Anthology Film Archives with support from The Film Foundation. Special thanks to Cineric, Inc., and Trackwise.“The film consists of four parts. The first part contains some footage from my first years in America, 1949-52. The second part was shot in August 1971 in Lithuania. The third part is in Elmshorn, near Hamburg, where I spent eight months in a forced labor camp. The fourth part is in Vienna (1971) with Peter Kubelka, [Hermann] Nitsch, Annette Michelson, Ken Jacobs, etc. The film deals with home, memory, and culture.” –Jonas MekasCLICK HERE TO BOOK TICKETS NOW!
